title: Kinetic and potential energy — the energy stores
subject: Physics
examTip: Energy store equations appear on every exam paper. Know each equation and its units. You must learn Ek = ½mv² and Ep = mgh. You are given Ee = ½ke² and ΔE = mcΔθ. Know what happens when energy moves between stores. The v² in the kinetic energy equation loses the most marks.
introTips: Today you will learn four energy equations: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential and specific heat capacity. Each one links a store to the situation that creates it.
The skill examiners test most is rearranging these equations and picking the right one. You will also practise setting GPE equal to KE to find the speed of a falling object.

Specific heat capacity is in this topic too. It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. It looks scary, but it is just one equation, used in a very predictable way.
intro: Every time you kick a ball, stretch a spring or drop your phone, energy moves between stores. This topic is about those stores. It is also about working out exactly how much energy is in them. You will use these equations in almost every physics paper. So the time you spend on them now pays back again and again. The maths isn't hard once you know which equation to use.

keyPoints.heading: Kinetic energy — the energy of movement
keyPoints.content: Anything that moves has kinetic energy (KE). The equation is: Ek = ½mv². Here m is mass in kg and v is speed in m/s. The answer comes out in joules (J). The key thing to notice is that v is squared. So if you double the speed, you quadruple the kinetic energy. A car doing 60 mph doesn't have twice the KE of a car doing 30 mph. It has four times as much. Exams often test whether you understand this. It is also why motorway crashes are so much more dangerous than town crashes.
writeBullets: Kinetic energy equation: Ek = ½mv²
m = mass in kg; v = speed in m/s; Ek in joules (J)
v is squared. Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy
To find v from Ek: rearrange to v = √(2Ek ÷ m)

keyTerms.def: The energy an object has due to its motion; Ek = ½mv², where m is mass (kg) and v is speed (m/s); measured in joules (J)
The SI unit of energy and work — 1 J = 1 N m = the energy transferred when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force

keyPoints.memTip: Ek = ½mv² — 'half em vee squared'. If speed doubles, KE quadruples (2² = 4); if speed triples, KE multiplies by 9 (3² = 9).

keyPoints.heading: Gravitational potential energy — the energy of height
keyPoints.content: When you lift something up, you give it gravitational potential energy (GPE). The equation is: Ep = mgh. - m is mass in kg - g is gravitational field strength in N/kg. It is about 9.8 N/kg on Earth. Always use the value of g given in the question - h is height in metres The answer is in joules. GPE goes up in step with height and mass. Double the height, and you double the GPE. That is simpler than kinetic energy, because nothing is squared.
writeBullets: GPE equation: Ep = mgh
m = mass (kg), g = gravitational field strength (N/kg), h = height (m). Use the value of g given in the question
GPE in joules (J)
Double the height → double the GPE (linear relationship)

keyTerms.def: Energy stored in an object due to its height above a reference point; Ep = mgh, where m is mass (kg), g is gravitational field strength (N/kg), and h is height (m); measured in joules (J)
The gravitational force acting per unit mass; about 9.8 N/kg on Earth's surface — always use the value given in the question; unit: N/kg

keyPoints.memTip: Ep = mgh — 'My Gran's High'. Double the height → double the GPE (linear, no squaring).

keyPoints.heading: Conservation of energy — GPE becomes KE
keyPoints.content: Energy can't be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred between stores. Picture an object falling, ignoring air resistance. All the energy in the gravitational potential store at the top is transferred to the kinetic store at the bottom. Halfway down, half of this energy has been transferred to the kinetic store. So you can set the two equations equal to find the speed at the bottom: mgh = ½mv². The mass cancels from both sides, leaving gh = ½v². So v = √(2gh). This is a classic calculation. It looks scary, but it is just substituting, then rearranging.
writeBullets: Conservation of energy: energy is never created or destroyed. It is only transferred
Falling object (no air resistance): energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store
At the top: all GPE. At the bottom: all KE
Equate: mgh = ½mv² → mass cancels → v = √(2gh)

keyTerms.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between stores or dissipated; the total energy in a closed system remains constant
The movement of energy from one store to another (e.g. gravitational potential → kinetic as an object falls), or the spreading of energy as dissipation

keyPoints.memTip: Falling object (no air resistance): all GPE at top → all KE at bottom. mgh = ½mv², cancel m, get v = √(2gh).

keyPoints.heading: Elastic potential energy — energy stored in a stretched spring
keyPoints.content: When you stretch or squash a spring, energy is stored in it as elastic potential energy. The same is true for a rubber band, or anything elastic. The equation is: Ee = ½ke². It only works if the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. - k is the spring constant in N/m. It measures how stiff the spring is - e is the extension in metres Note that e is the extension, not the total length. It is how far the spring has stretched beyond its natural length. As with kinetic energy, e is squared. So doubling the extension quadruples the elastic PE.
writeBullets: Elastic PE equation: Ee = ½ke². Only if the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded
k = spring constant (N/m); e = extension in metres (not total length)
e is squared. Double the extension → four times the elastic PE
Elastic PE is in joules (J)

keyTerms.def: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object; Ee = ½ke², where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is the extension (m); measured in joules (J)
A measure of the stiffness of a spring; k = F ÷ e, where F is the force (N) and e is the extension (m); unit: N/m — higher k means a stiffer spring
The increase in length of a spring beyond its natural (unstretched) length; e = stretched length − natural length; measured in metres (m)

keyPoints.memTip: Ee = ½ke² has the same shape as Ek = ½mv². Both are ½ × something × (something)². e is extension only, not total length. Examiners use this to catch you out.

keyPoints.heading: Specific heat capacity — energy per kilogram per degree
keyPoints.content: Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm up. The specific heat capacity (c) of a material is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of it by 1°C. The equation is: ΔE = mcΔθ. - ΔE is the change in thermal energy in joules - m is mass in kg - c is specific heat capacity in J/kg°C - Δθ is the temperature change in °C The same equation gives the energy released when a system cools. Water's specific heat capacity is 4200 J/kg°C. That is very high. It is why water is used as a coolant in car engines. It is also why the sea takes a long time to warm up in summer.
writeBullets: Specific heat capacity equation: ΔE = mcΔθ
ΔE = change in thermal energy (J), m = mass (kg), c = specific heat capacity (J/kg°C), Δθ = temperature change (°C)
High c means the material needs more energy per kg per °C to heat up
Water: c = 4200 J/kg°C. Very high, so useful as a coolant

keyTerms.def: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C — units J/kg°C
The change in temperature (final temperature minus initial temperature) in °C

keyPoints.memTip: ΔE = mcΔθ is a favourite rearrangement question. Cover each letter in turn. Practise writing each rearrangement: c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ), m = ΔE ÷ (cΔθ), Δθ = ΔE ÷ (mc).

0.question: A 2 kg ball is moving at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Ek = ½ × 2 × 3² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. Remember to square v before multiplying.
0.wrongFeedback: Use Ek = ½mv². Here: ½ × 2 × 3² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J. The most common mistake is forgetting to square v first. Always deal with v² before multiplying by m.

1.question: A 5 kg bag is lifted to a height of 3 m. Using g = 10 N/kg, what is its gravitational potential energy?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. GPE = mgh = 5 x 10 x 3 = 150 J. Mass in kg, g in N/kg and height in m give energy in joules.
1.wrongFeedback: Use GPE = mgh. Here: 5 kg x 10 N/kg x 3 m = 150 J. A common mistake is not multiplying all three values together. The formula has three variables, not two.

2.question: A ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Ignore air resistance. What is its speed just before it hits the ground? (g = 10 N/kg)
2.correctFeedback: Correct. v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 5) = √100 = 10 m/s. All the energy in the gravitational potential store is transferred to the kinetic store. The masses cancel, leaving v = √(2gh).
2.wrongFeedback: Equate GPE and KE: mgh = ½mv². Masses cancel: gh = ½v². So v² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100. Therefore v = √100 = 10 m/s.

3.question: A spring with spring constant k = 400 N/m is stretched by 0.05 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored?
3.correctFeedback: Correct. Ee = ½ke² = 0.5 × 400 × (0.05)² = 0.5 × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.5 J. Remember to square the extension before multiplying.
3.wrongFeedback: Use Ee = ½ke². Extension e = 0.05 m. e² = 0.0025. Then: 0.5 × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.5 J. The most common mistake is forgetting to square the extension.

4.question: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 0.5 kg of water by 10°C? (c = 4200 J/kg°C)
4.wrongFeedback: Use ΔE = mcΔθ. Multiply all three values: 0.5 × 4200 × 10 = 21,000 J.

commonMistakes: In Ek = ½mv², square v before multiplying by anything else. For a 2 kg object at 4 m/s: Ek = ½ × 2 × 16 = 16 J (not ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 J).
The question always gives you the value of g. Use that value, whether it is 9.8 N/kg or 10 N/kg.

In the elastic PE equation Ee = ½ke², e is the extension. It is how far the spring has stretched beyond its natural length. Say a spring is 0.3 m long naturally and is stretched to 0.5 m. Then e = 0.2 m, not 0.5 m.

When a falling object hits the ground, all its GPE has become KE only if air resistance is ignored. If the question mentions air resistance, some energy has gone to thermal stores. Then you cannot simply set mgh = ½mv².
In ΔE = mcΔθ, Δθ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature. If an object heats from 20°C to 80°C, Δθ = 60°C.
examTips: Always show the equation, substitution and answer on separate lines. Mark schemes give method marks at each stage.
A question may say 'ignoring air resistance' or 'no energy dissipated to the surroundings'. Then set GPE = KE at the bottom: mgh = ½mv². This simplifies to v = √(2gh).
For specific heat capacity, check which you need: ΔE (change in thermal energy), m (mass), c or Δθ. Rearrange before substituting. Don't try to rearrange after putting numbers in.
revisionCardBullets: Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv². m in kg, v in m/s, Ek in J
Double the speed → quadruple the KE (because v is squared)
Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh. Use the value of g given in the question
Falling object (no air resistance). By the bottom, all the energy in the gravitational potential store is transferred to the kinetic store
Equate GPE and KE: mgh = ½mv² → mass cancels → v = √(2gh)
Elastic PE: Ee = ½ke² (if the limit of proportionality is not exceeded). k = spring constant (N/m). e = extension in metres (not total length)
Specific heat capacity: ΔE = mcΔθ. ΔE in J, m in kg, c in J/kg°C. Δθ = temperature change in °C
Water's specific heat capacity = 4200 J/kg°C. Very high, so it is used as a coolant
